title: Formula size versus partition complexity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Are there universal constants \(C\ge1\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every nonconstant Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every \(n\ge1\), satisfies \(L(f)\le C\,\chi(f)^d\)? Here \(L(f)\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size, and \(\chi(f)\) is the minimum number of disjoint coordinate-monochromatic rectangles partitioning \(f^{-1}(1)\times f^{-1}(0)\). The polynomial bound must depend only on \(\chi(f)\), with no additional factor depending on \(n\).
why: A formula organizes computation hierarchically, whereas a rectangle partition only gives a disjoint collection of valid local distinctions between accepting and rejecting inputs. The question asks whether this absence of an imposed hierarchy can yield more than polynomial savings. A resolution would determine how closely a central combinatorial lower-bound measure captures general formula size.
status_note: The primary second-edition author draft dated 14 September 2026 explicitly retains the polynomial inverse as an open Research Problem 6.1 and states the quasipolynomial bound. Bounded checks through 2026-09-16 found no newer resolution of the exact measure. The draft’s date and status are recorded without implying publication or an exhaustive proof audit.

sentences: A De Morgan formula computes a Boolean function with an expression tree whose leaves are literals.
Its partition measure counts disjoint rectangles pairing accepting and rejecting inputs, each certified by one differing coordinate.
The question asks whether formula leaf size is always bounded by a fixed polynomial in that rectangle count.
The partition need not already be organized as a recursive communication protocol, which is the source of the possible gap.
Jukna’s author draft dated 14 September 2026 still lists the polynomial inverse as open and gives only a quasipolynomial general bound.

definitions: A De Morgan formula on \(n\) variables is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is AND or OR; each leaf is one literal \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Evaluation uses the usual Boolean operations. Repeated occurrences of the same literal count as separate leaves, and subtrees cannot be shared. The leaf size is the total number of leaves. Define \(L(f)\) as the minimum leaf size among formulas evaluating to \(f(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Formulas need not be monotone, balanced, depth-bounded or uniformly constructible. Let \(A=f^{-1}(1)\) and \(B=f^{-1}(0)\), both nonempty because \(f\) is nonconstant. A rectangle is a nonempty Cartesian product \(U\times V\) with \(U\subseteq A\) and \(V\subseteq B\). It is coordinate-monochromatic if there are a coordinate \(i\in[n]\) and a bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(u_i=b\) for every \(u\in U\) and \(v_i=1-b\) for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, a single literal separates the two sides, with either orientation permitted. A partition is a finite collection of such rectangles whose union is all of \(A\times B\), with distinct rectangles pairwise disjoint as subsets of ordered pairs. Row sets may overlap across rectangles, and column sets may overlap, provided the products do not. Define \(\chi(f)\) as the minimum number of rectangles in any such partition; coordinate labels and the descriptions of the row and column sets have no additional cost. Every pair \(a\in A,b\in B\) differs in some coordinate, so a singleton partition exists and \(\chi(f)\ge1\) is finite. No recursive or protocol-tree condition is imposed on a partition. The statement quantifies \(\exists C,d\;\forall n\;\forall f\) with the domains above. Both measures are nonuniform finite mathematical minima; no algorithm converting a partition into a formula is required. Restricting to nonconstant functions removes the empty-rectangle convention for constants without changing the substantive comparison.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a universal polynomial bound \(L(f)\le C\chi(f)^d\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\forall C\ge1\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\exists n\ge1\;\exists f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) nonconstant with \(L(f)>C\chi(f)^d\). Refuting one proposed exponent or giving a constant-factor gap is insufficient to refute all polynomial bounds. A result for arbitrary communication relations, overlapping covers, positively oriented monotone partitions or algebraic tilings does not automatically establish the target for the defined partitions of total Boolean functions.

context_blocks.text: The imported early draft states the question as Research Problem 6.24 after Rychkov’s lemma. Its tiling number is a coordinate-labelled partition of accepting versus rejecting inputs, rather than a partition of the Boolean input cube or a tiling by constant output bits.

Rychkov’s lemma gives \(\chi(f)\le L(f)\). The question asks whether the reverse comparison holds with one fixed polynomial for every Boolean function. The known bound recorded by the source is \(L(f)\le\chi(f)^{2\log_2\chi(f)}\), which is quasipolynomial rather than polynomial.

Disjointness is essential to the measure: overlapping coordinate rectangles can cover every accepting–rejecting pair using only twice the number of variables. The task concerns the minimum disjoint partition, not the size of such an unrestricted cover.

Neither the formulas nor the functions are required to be monotone. Both orientations of a differing coordinate are allowed in a partition rectangle. The source separately defines positively monochromatic partitions for monotone formula questions.

Jukna’s second expanded edition draft dated 14 September 2026 retains the exact question as Research Problem 6.1 on printed page 277. It again states that the polynomial inverse is unknown and records the same quasipolynomial upper bound. This is a dated author draft, not a claim of publication of the second edition.
